title: Network Security and Wireless Fundamentals
subtitle: Protect a Cisco network from the router to the access port: harden device access, filter traffic with ACLs, stop Layer 2 attacks, and build wireless LANs secured with WPA2 and WPA3.
outcomes: Explain threats, vulnerabilities and exploits, and choose mitigations for them
Secure access to Cisco devices with strong secrets, SSH and AAA
Write, apply and verify standard and extended access control lists
Protect access ports with port security, DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection
Compare wireless architectures, from autonomous access points to wireless LAN controllers
Configure a WLAN secured with WPA2 on a wireless LAN controller, and explain what WPA3 adds
prerequisites: Basic Cisco IOS configuration and IPv4 addressing with subnet masks, and an idea of what VLANs and DHCP do. Install Cisco Packet Tracer (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account) on Windows, macOS or Linux.
description:
This course teaches you to defend a network, layer by layer, on Cisco routers, switches and wireless controllers in Cisco Packet Tracer, following the Security Fundamentals topics of Cisco's CCNA (200-301) exam. You'll start with the language of security, threats, vulnerabilities, exploits and mitigations, and then protect the devices themselves: hashed secrets, local users, SSH, protection against password guessing, and AAA with a TACACS+ server. You'll turn a written policy into standard and extended access control lists, placed where they work best, and prove they do what you meant. At the access layer you'll stop the attacks that start at a wall socket, with port security, DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection. Finally you'll learn how Wi-Fi works, how enterprise wireless is built from access points and controllers, and how WPA2 and WPA3 protect it, and you'll configure a secure WLAN on a wireless LAN controller.

Everything here is defensive: you'll practise on your own simulated networks, and every module ends with a Packet Tracer lab that your instructor reviews. The capstone asks you to secure a whole branch office and write the security assessment an auditor would expect.
aligned_with: Cisco CCNA (200-301) exam topics: Security Fundamentals

modules.title: Security concepts and secure device access
modules.summary: The language of security, then the first thing to protect on any network: who can log in to its routers and switches, and how they prove who they are.

lessons.title: Threats, vulnerabilities, exploits and mitigations
objectives: Define threat, vulnerability, exploit and risk, and relate them to confidentiality, integrity and availability
Recognise common kinds of attack and the mitigations for each
Describe a security programme's people and physical elements: user awareness, training and physical access control
key_points: Security protects confidentiality (only the right people see data), integrity (data isn't changed without permission) and availability (systems work when they're needed), together called the CIA triad.

A vulnerability is a weakness, such as unpatched software or a default password; a threat is someone or something that could take advantage of it; an exploit is the method that does; risk weighs how likely that is against the harm it would cause.

Common attacks include malware, phishing and other social engineering, password guessing, denial of service (DoS and DDoS), address spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks, often after reconnaissance that maps the network.
Mitigations are layered, called defence in depth: patching, hardened devices, strong authentication, traffic filtering, encryption, and logging so attacks get noticed. No single control is enough.

A security programme also covers people and places: user awareness campaigns, regular training (such as spotting phishing), and physical access control, such as locked wiring closets and badge readers.
Least privilege gives each person and system only the access they need, so a stolen account or a mistake does less damage.

lessons.title: Passwords and local device access
objectives: Protect console, privileged and remote access with secrets and local users
Explain password policies, and alternatives such as multifactor authentication, certificates and biometrics
key_points: enable secret protects privileged EXEC mode with a hashed password. The older enable password is stored in clear text, and enable secret wins when both are set.
username NAME secret PASSWORD creates a local user stored as a hash; login local on a line then asks for a username and password instead of one shared line password.

service password-encryption scrambles clear-text passwords in the configuration as type 7, which is easily reversed, so it only stops someone reading over your shoulder. Secrets are real hashes: type 5 (MD5-based) on older IOS such as Packet Tracer's, and the stronger types 8 and 9 on newer IOS.

security passwords min-length sets a minimum length for new passwords, exec-timeout logs idle sessions out, and login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60 refuses logins for two minutes after three failures in one minute.
A password policy covers length (a long passphrase beats a short complicated password), no reuse, changing passwords after any compromise, and keeping them in a password manager, not in files.

Multifactor authentication combines something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or token) and something you are (a fingerprint); certificates and biometrics can replace passwords altogether.

steps.do: On R1, set a minimum password length, then a hashed enable secret.
steps.code:
configure terminal
security passwords min-length 10
enable secret Class-Lab-2026

steps.do: Create a local user, make the console ask for it, and log idle sessions out after five minutes.
steps.code:
username admin secret Lab-Admin-2026
line console 0
 login local
 exec-timeout 5 0
 exit

steps.do: Slow down password guessing, add a warning banner, and scramble any clear-text passwords.
steps.code:
login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
banner motd #Authorised access only. Activity may be monitored.#
service password-encryption
end

steps.do: See how the secrets are stored.
steps.code: show running-config | include secret
steps.see: enable secret 5 and username admin secret 5, each followed by a hash starting $1$, never the passwords themselves.

steps.do: Try a secret that's too short.
steps.code:
configure terminal
enable secret short1
steps.see: IOS rejects it as shorter than the minimum length.

steps.do: Type end and exit, press Enter, and log in again at the console.
steps.see: The banner, then a Username: prompt: the console now wants the local user.

lessons.title: AAA servers, and VPNs
objectives: Compare authentication, authorisation and accounting
Compare TACACS+ with RADIUS, and log in to a router through an AAA server
Describe site-to-site and remote-access IPsec VPNs
key_points: AAA answers three questions: authentication (who are you?), authorisation (what may you do?) and accounting (what did you do, and when?), which gives an audit trail.
Local AAA checks users stored on each device; server-based AAA checks a central server, so accounts are added and removed in one place. Keep a local user as a fallback for when no server answers.

TACACS+ (TCP port 49) encrypts the whole message and keeps authentication, authorisation and accounting separate, which suits controlling device administrators. RADIUS (UDP ports 1812 and 1813) encrypts only the password and combines authentication with authorisation; it's the usual choice for 802.1X and Wi-Fi.

aaa new-model turns AAA on, and aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local tries the TACACS+ server first, falling back to local users only when no server answers, not when the server says no.

A VPN carries private traffic across a public network in an encrypted tunnel. Site-to-site VPNs join whole networks through gateways such as routers or firewalls; remote-access VPNs connect one person's device, with VPN client software or through a browser.

IPsec protects VPN traffic with confidentiality (encryption such as AES), integrity (hashes such as SHA), peer authentication (pre-shared keys or certificates) and anti-replay protection; IKE negotiates the keys.

walkthrough.title: Log in through a TACACS+ server

steps.do: Click the AAA server (192.168.1.2), open Services | AAA and turn the service On. Under Network Configuration add a client: Client Name R1, Client IP 192.168.1.1, Secret tacacs-lab-key, Server Type Tacacs. Click Add.
Under User Setup, add the user netadmin with the password Net-Admin-2026, and click Add.
On R1, keep a local user for emergencies, point R1 at the server, and turn on AAA with the server first and local users as the fallback.
steps.code:
configure terminal
username admin secret Lab-Admin-2026
tacacs-server host 192.168.1.2 key tacacs-lab-key
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
end

steps.do: Type exit and log in at the console as netadmin, the user that exists only on the server.
steps.see: The login succeeds: R1 asked the TACACS+ server.

steps.do: Turn the server's AAA service Off. Log in as netadmin again, then as admin.
steps.see: netadmin fails, because the fallback is R1's own users, and admin gets in.

steps.do: Turn the AAA service back On.

lab.title: Harden a router's management access
lab.goal: Lock down how administrators reach a router: hashed secrets and local users, SSH only, protection against password guessing, and logins checked by a TACACS+ server with a local fallback.
setup: Cisco Packet Tracer 8 or later (free with a Cisco Networking Academy account)
The starter file r1-base.txt and the addressing table in addressing.txt

steps.do: Build the topology from addressing.txt: R1 (2911) g0/0 to S1 (2960) g0/1, with the AAA server on f0/1 and Admin-PC on f0/2. Paste r1-base.txt into R1 and give the server and the PC their static addresses.
Set the password rules, secrets and banner on R1.
steps.code:
configure terminal
security passwords min-length 10
enable secret Class-Lab-2026
username admin secret Lab-Admin-2026
service password-encryption
banner motd #Authorised access only. Activity may be monitored.#

steps.do: Protect the console and refuse logins after repeated failures.
steps.code:
line console 0
 login local
 exec-timeout 5 0
 exit
login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60

steps.do: Allow SSH version 2 only on the vty lines. Answer 2048 when asked for the modulus.
steps.code:
ip domain-name example.com
crypto key generate rsa
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
 exec-timeout 5 0
 end

steps.do: On the AAA server, turn on Services | AAA, add R1 as a Tacacs client (192.168.1.1, secret tacacs-lab-key) and add the user netadmin (Net-Admin-2026).
Send R1's logins to the server, with its local users as the fallback.
steps.code:
configure terminal
tacacs-server host 192.168.1.2 key tacacs-lab-key
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
end

steps.do: From Admin-PC's Command Prompt, log in over SSH as netadmin, then type exit.
steps.code: ssh -l netadmin 192.168.1.1
steps.see: A Password: prompt, the banner and then R1>.

steps.do: Turn the server's AAA service Off. From Admin-PC, try SSH as netadmin and then as admin. Turn the service back On afterwards.
steps.code:
ssh -l netadmin 192.168.1.1
ssh -l admin 192.168.1.1
steps.see: netadmin is refused and admin gets in.

steps.do: Collect the evidence from R1.
steps.code:
show running-config
show ip ssh
steps.see: Secrets as type 5 hashes, line passwords as type 7, the aaa and tacacs-server lines, login block-for, transport input ssh, and SSH Enabled - version 2.0.

checks.text: Privileged EXEC and the local user are protected by secrets, stored as hashes rather than passwords.
Logins are refused for a while after repeated failures.
SSH version 2 is the only way in over the network.
Logins go to the TACACS+ server first, with local users as the fallback, and netadmin logs in through the server.
look_for: aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local

checks.text: A sentence explains why, with the server down, admin got in and netadmin didn't.

lab.submit: Paste R1's running configuration, show ip ssh, the SSH attempts from Admin-PC with the server on and off, and a sentence explaining why admin got in and netadmin didn't while the server was off.

files.content:
enable
configure terminal
hostname R1
no ip domain-lookup
interface g0/0
 description Management LAN
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
end

Lab 1 addressing

Device      Interface       Address         Mask            Gateway       Connects to
R1          g0/0            192.168.1.1     255.255.255.0   -             S1 g0/1
AAA-Server  FastEthernet0   192.168.1.2     255.255.255.0   192.168.1.1   S1 f0/1
Admin-PC    FastEthernet0   192.168.1.10    255.255.255.0   192.168.1.1   S1 f0/2

Accounts used in the lab (choose your own on real equipment):
  enable secret                 Class-Lab-2026
  local user on R1              admin / Lab-Admin-2026
  TACACS+ key (R1 and server)   tacacs-lab-key
  user on the TACACS+ server    netadmin / Net-Admin-2026

hints: If every SSH login fails after aaa new-model, check that the key on R1 matches the server's Secret exactly, and that the server's client entry is 192.168.1.1 with Server Type Tacacs.
If you lock yourself out with login block-for, wait the 120 seconds and try again.
A secret rejected as too short is security passwords min-length doing its job: choose a longer one.

modules.title: Access control lists
modules.summary: Filter traffic with standard and extended ACLs: how a router reads them, how to write wildcard masks, where to apply them, and how to prove they do what you meant.

lessons.title: How ACLs work: order, wildcard masks and placement
objectives: Explain how a router checks a packet against an ACL
Write wildcard masks for hosts, subnets and ranges
Decide where to apply standard and extended ACLs
key_points: An ACL is a list of permit and deny statements checked from the top: the first match decides and the rest are skipped. Every ACL ends with an unseen deny any, so an ACL of only deny statements blocks everything.
A wildcard mask says which address bits must match: 0 means must match and 1 means ignore. 0.0.0.255 matches a /24, the keyword host means 0.0.0.0 (one address), and any means 255.255.255.255.
To turn a subnet mask into a wildcard, subtract each octet from 255: a /26 (255.255.255.192) needs 0.0.0.63, so 192.168.10.64 0.0.0.63 matches 192.168.10.64 to 192.168.10.127.

Standard ACLs (numbers 1-99 and 1300-1999) match only the source address; extended ACLs (100-199 and 2000-2699) match the protocol, source and destination addresses and ports. Named ACLs of either kind are easier to read and edit.

An interface takes one ACL per direction for each protocol: inbound ACLs filter packets before they're routed, outbound ACLs after. Put standard ACLs close to the destination and extended ACLs close to the source.
Order statements from the most specific to the most general: a broad permit near the top hides every statement below it.

lessons.title: Standard ACLs, numbered and named
objectives: Configure numbered and named standard ACLs and apply them to interfaces
Restrict SSH access to a device with an ACL on its vty lines
Verify ACLs with their match counters
key_points: access-list 10 deny 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 followed by access-list 10 permit any blocks one subnet and allows the rest; without the permit any, the unseen deny would block everything.
ip access-list standard NAME opens a named ACL. Its statements get sequence numbers (10, 20, 30 and so on), so you can insert a statement between two others, or delete one by its number.
ip access-group NAME in (or out) applies an ACL to an interface. access-class NAME in applies a standard ACL to the vty lines, deciding which addresses may open SSH sessions to the device itself.
show access-lists shows every ACL with a match count for each statement, show ip interface shows which ACLs an interface uses, and clear access-list counters starts the counts again.
A remark line, such as remark Admin PC only, records why a statement is there for the next person who reads it.

walkthrough.title: Let only the admin PC manage R1

steps.do: On R1, create a named standard ACL that permits only the admin PC.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip access-list standard VTY-ADMIN
 remark Only Admin-PC may manage R1
 permit host 192.168.10.10
 exit

steps.do: Apply it to the vty lines.
steps.code:
line vty 0 4
 access-class VTY-ADMIN in
 end

steps.do: Open an SSH session to R1 from Admin-PC, then from another PC.
steps.code: ssh -l admin 192.168.10.1
steps.see: Admin-PC gets a Password: prompt; the other PC's connection is refused.

steps.do: Look at the counters.
steps.code: show access-lists
steps.see: Standard IP access list VTY-ADMIN, with a match count beside the permit statement.

steps.do: Insert a statement for a second admin PC by giving it a sequence number, then look again.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip access-list standard VTY-ADMIN
 15 permit host 192.168.10.12
 end
show access-lists
steps.see: The new statement listed with sequence number 15, after 10.

lessons.title: Extended ACLs: protocols and ports
objectives: Write extended ACL statements that match protocols, addresses and ports
Allow the traffic a group of users needs, and block the rest
key_points: An extended statement gives a protocol (ip, tcp, udp or icmp), then the source, then the destination, then optionally a port: permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 80.
Common ports: FTP 20 and 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, DHCP 67 and 68, TFTP 69, HTTP 80, NTP 123, SNMP 161 and 162, HTTPS 443 and syslog 514.
Port operators include eq, neq, lt, gt and range. IOS shows well-known ports by name, so eq 80 appears as eq www and eq 53 as eq domain.
Without a final permit, the unseen deny blocks all other traffic, including traffic you may not have thought of, such as routing protocol messages and DHCP requests, which come from 0.0.0.0.
Apply an extended ACL inbound on the interface nearest the traffic's source, so the router drops unwanted packets before they cross the network.
Test both what should work and what shouldn't, and read the match counters: a statement whose count never rises is redundant or in the wrong place.

walkthrough.title: Let guests use the web server and nothing else

steps.do: On R1, write a named extended ACL for traffic arriving from the guest LAN.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
 remark Guests: DNS and the web server only, nothing else in the Server LAN
 permit udp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 53
 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 80
 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 443
 deny ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.30.0 0.0.0.255
 permit ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 any
 exit

steps.do: Apply it inbound on the guest LAN's interface, close to the source.
steps.code:
interface g0/1
 ip access-group GUEST-IN in
 end

steps.do: From Guest-PC, open http://www.example.com in the Web Browser, then ping the server.
steps.see: The page loads by name, but the pings fail with Destination host unreachable.

steps.do: See which statements matched.
steps.code: show access-lists
steps.see: Matches on the eq domain and eq www statements from browsing, and on the deny statement from the pings.

steps.do: Check the interface is using the ACL.
steps.code: show ip interface g0/1
steps.see: Inbound access list is GUEST-IN

lab.title: Filter traffic with standard and extended ACLs
lab.goal: Turn a written security policy into three ACLs: a standard ACL that keeps guests out of the staff LAN, an extended ACL that lets guests use only the web server and DNS, and a vty ACL that lets only the admin PC manage the router.
setup: The starter file r1-base.txt, and addressing.txt with the addressing and the policy

steps.do: Build the topology from addressing.txt: R1 (2911) with a 2960 switch on each of g0/0, g0/1 and g0/2, and the hosts on the switches. Paste r1-base.txt into R1, give the hosts their addresses, and on the Server turn on DNS with the A record www.example.com for 192.168.30.10.
Finish SSH on R1: generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair and use version 2.
steps.code:
configure terminal
crypto key generate rsa
ip ssh version 2
end

steps.do: Test before filtering: from Guest-PC, ping Staff-PC (192.168.10.11) and the Server (192.168.30.10).
steps.see: Both reply: with no ACLs, R1 routes everything.

steps.do: Keep guests out of the staff LAN with a standard ACL, applied outbound on the interface nearest the staff LAN.
steps.code:
configure terminal
access-list 10 remark Keep the guest LAN out of the staff LAN
access-list 10 deny 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 10 permit any
interface g0/0
 ip access-group 10 out
 end

steps.do: Write GUEST-IN so guests can use DNS, HTTP and HTTPS on the server and nothing else in the Server LAN, while other traffic from them is allowed. Apply it inbound on g0/1.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
 permit udp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 53
 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 80
 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq 443
 deny ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.30.0 0.0.0.255
 permit ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 any
 exit
interface g0/1
 ip access-group GUEST-IN in
 end

steps.do: Let only Admin-PC open SSH sessions to R1.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip access-list standard VTY-ADMIN
 permit host 192.168.10.10
 exit
line vty 0 4
 access-class VTY-ADMIN in
 end

steps.do: Test the policy from Guest-PC: browse to http://www.example.com, then ping the Server and Staff-PC.
steps.see: The web page loads; both pings fail with Destination host unreachable.

steps.do: Test management: SSH to 192.168.10.1 as admin from Admin-PC, then from Staff-PC.
steps.see: Admin-PC gets a Password: prompt; Staff-PC's connection is refused.

steps.do: Collect the evidence on R1.
steps.code:
show access-lists
show ip interface g0/0
show ip interface g0/1
steps.see: Match counts on the statements you tested, Outgoing access list is 10 on g0/0 and Inbound access list is GUEST-IN on g0/1.

steps.do: Think it through: from Staff-PC, ping Guest-PC (192.168.20.11). It fails, though the policy says nothing about staff reaching guests. Find out which ACL stops it, and why.

checks.text: A standard ACL, applied outbound towards the staff LAN, keeps guests out of it.
GUEST-IN lets guests use the web server and DNS, and is applied inbound on the guest interface.
Pings from Guest-PC to the Server and to Staff-PC fail.
Only Admin-PC can open an SSH session to R1.
A sentence explains that Staff-PC's ping fails because ACL 10 drops Guest-PC's replies, since a standard ACL sees only the source address, not who started the conversation.

lab.submit: Paste show access-lists, show ip interface for g0/0 and g0/1, Guest-PC's pings, the SSH attempts from Admin-PC and Staff-PC, and your explanation of why Staff-PC can't ping Guest-PC.

files.content:
enable
configure terminal
hostname R1
no ip domain-lookup
ip domain-name example.com
username admin secret Lab-Admin-2026
interface g0/0
 description Staff LAN
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
interface g0/1
 description Guest LAN
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
interface g0/2
 description Server LAN
 ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
 exit
end

Lab 2 addressing

Device     Interface       Address          Mask            Gateway         Connects to
R1         g0/0            192.168.10.1     255.255.255.0   -               S1 g0/1  (Staff LAN)
R1         g0/1            192.168.20.1     255.255.255.0   -               S2 g0/1  (Guest LAN)
R1         g0/2            192.168.30.1     255.255.255.0   -               S3 g0/1  (Server LAN)
Admin-PC   FastEthernet0   192.168.10.10    255.255.255.0   192.168.10.1    S1 f0/1
Staff-PC   FastEthernet0   192.168.10.11    255.255.255.0   192.168.10.1    S1 f0/2
Guest-PC   FastEthernet0   192.168.20.11    255.255.255.0   192.168.20.1    S2 f0/1
Server     FastEthernet0   192.168.30.10    255.255.255.0   192.168.30.1    S3 f0/1  (HTTP, HTTPS and DNS on)

Every host uses 192.168.30.10 as its DNS server.
Add a DNS A record on Server: www.example.com -> 192.168.30.10

The policy to build:
  1. Guests may not reach the Staff LAN at all (standard ACL 10, outbound on g0/0).
  2. Guests may use DNS, HTTP and HTTPS on the server, and nothing else in the Server LAN
     (extended ACL GUEST-IN, inbound on g0/1). Anything else they send, such as to the internet, is allowed.
  3. Only Admin-PC may open SSH sessions to R1 (standard ACL VTY-ADMIN on the vty lines).

hints: If everything stops working after an ACL goes on, look for the final permit: every ACL ends with an unseen deny any.
To change a numbered ACL, it's simplest to remove it (no access-list 10) and type it again. Named ACLs let you delete or insert single statements by sequence number.
If the guest can't load the page by name, check GUEST-IN permits udp eq 53 to the Server, and that Guest-PC's DNS server is 192.168.30.10.

modules.title: Layer 2 security: port security, DHCP snooping and ARP inspection
modules.summary: Protect the access layer, where people plug in: limit which devices can use each port, stop rogue DHCP servers, and block ARP spoofing.

lessons.title: Port security
objectives: Limit the MAC addresses allowed on an access port
Choose a violation mode, and recover a port that has shut itself down
key_points: Port security limits which MAC addresses may send through a switch port. It works on access ports, so the port needs switchport mode access first, and it allows one address unless switchport port-security maximum raises the limit.

Allowed addresses can be typed in (static), learned and forgotten when the port goes down (dynamic), or learned and written into the running configuration with switchport port-security mac-address sticky.
Violation modes: shutdown, the default, puts the port in the err-disabled state; restrict drops the offending frames, logs them and counts violations; protect drops them without logging.
An err-disabled port stays down until you shut it and bring it back (shutdown, then no shutdown), or until errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation brings it back after a timer.
show port-security interface f0/1 shows the port status (Secure-up or Secure-shutdown), the violation mode, the maximum and the violation count; show port-security address lists the secure addresses.
Shut down unused ports and put them in an unused VLAN, so nobody can plug into a live one.

walkthrough.title: Secure a port and trigger a violation

steps.do: On S1, make f0/1 an access port and turn on port security, allowing one sticky address.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface f0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 1
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security violation shutdown
 end

steps.do: From PC1, on f0/1, ping the gateway so the switch learns PC1's MAC address. Then check the port.
steps.code:
show port-security interface f0/1
show port-security address
steps.see: Port Status Secure-up, and PC1's MAC address listed as a sticky secure address.

steps.do: Unplug PC1, plug a laptop into f0/1 instead, and ping the gateway from the laptop.
steps.see: The pings fail and the link goes red: the switch has shut the port down.

steps.do: Look at the port now.
steps.code:
show port-security interface f0/1
show interfaces status
steps.see: Port Status Secure-shutdown, a Security Violation Count of 1, and err-disabled in the status list.

steps.do: Reconnect PC1 and recover the port.
steps.code:
configure terminal
interface f0/1
 shutdown
 no shutdown
 end
steps.see: Secure-up again once PC1 sends.

lessons.title: DHCP snooping
objectives: Explain how a rogue DHCP server harms a network, and how DHCP snooping stops it
Configure trusted and untrusted ports and read the binding table
key_points: A rogue DHCP server, malicious or just a misconfigured home router, can answer clients first and give its own address as their gateway or DNS server, putting itself in the middle of their traffic or cutting them off.

With DHCP snooping on, every port is untrusted until you trust it: the switch drops DHCP server messages, such as offers and acknowledgements, that arrive on untrusted ports. Trust only ports towards real DHCP servers and uplinks.

Turn it on globally with ip dhcp snooping and for each VLAN with ip dhcp snooping vlan 1; ip dhcp snooping trust trusts a port, and ip dhcp snooping limit rate caps DHCP messages per second on an untrusted port.
The switch records every lease it sees in a binding table: MAC address, IP address, lease time, VLAN and port. Dynamic ARP inspection and IP Source Guard check traffic against it.

By default the switch inserts option 82 into requests without a relay address, and an IOS router acting as the DHCP server drops such requests: no ip dhcp snooping information option on the switch, or ip dhcp relay information trust-all on the router, fixes it.
show ip dhcp snooping shows the VLANs and the trusted ports, and show ip dhcp snooping binding lists the bindings.

steps.do: On S1, turn on DHCP snooping, for VLAN 1 too.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 1

steps.do: Trust only the port to the real DHCP server (f0/24) and the uplink to the router (g0/1), and limit DHCP messages on the PC ports.

interface f0/24
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 exit
interface g0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 exit
interface range f0/1 - 2

 end

steps.do: On each PC's Command Prompt, give up its address and ask again.
steps.code:
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
steps.see: An address from the real server's range, with gateway 192.168.1.1: the rogue's offers are dropped at its untrusted port.

steps.do: Check the switch's view.

show ip dhcp snooping
show ip dhcp snooping binding
steps.see: Switch DHCP snooping is enabled, f0/24 and g0/1 trusted, and a dhcp-snooping binding for each PC with its port.

lessons.title: Dynamic ARP inspection
objectives: Explain how ARP spoofing redirects traffic
Configure dynamic ARP inspection with trusted ports, and verify it
key_points: ARP has no authentication, so any host can send an ARP reply nobody asked for (a gratuitous ARP) claiming the gateway's IP address. Hosts that believe it send their traffic to that host instead: ARP spoofing, or ARP poisoning.

Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI) checks ARP packets arriving on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table, and drops any whose MAC and IP addresses don't match a binding. It needs DHCP snooping running first.

ip arp inspection vlan 1 turns it on for a VLAN, and ip arp inspection trust trusts a port. Trust uplinks and the ports of devices with static addresses, or permit those devices with an ARP access list, or their ARP packets are dropped.
ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip adds checks that the MAC addresses inside each ARP packet match its Ethernet header, and that its IP addresses are valid.
Untrusted ports may send 15 ARP packets a second by default; a port that sends more is err-disabled, which also stops ARP floods.
show ip arp inspection shows how many ARP packets were forwarded and dropped, and show ip arp inspection interfaces shows each port's trust state and rate limit.

steps.do: Support for dynamic ARP inspection varies between Packet Tracer versions. If your 2960 doesn't accept the ip arp inspection commands, follow these steps as a reading exercise: they work as shown on Catalyst switches. Start with DHCP snooping running on VLAN 1, as in the previous lesson.
Turn on DAI for VLAN 1.
steps.code:
configure terminal
ip arp inspection vlan 1

steps.do: Trust the uplink to the router and the DHCP server's port: both have static addresses, so neither is in the binding table.
steps.code:
interface g0/1
 ip arp inspection trust
 exit
interface f0/24
 ip arp inspection trust
 exit

steps.do: Add the extra address checks.
steps.code:
ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip
end

steps.do: Ping the gateway from a PC that got its address by DHCP, then from a host with a static address on an untrusted port.
steps.see: The DHCP client's pings succeed; the static host's fail, because its ARP requests match no binding.

steps.do: Read the counters and the ports' trust states.
steps.code:
show ip arp inspection
show ip arp inspection interfaces
steps.see: Forwarded and dropped counts for VLAN 1, and g0/1 and f0/24 as Trusted.

lab.goal: Secure the access switch where users plug in: shut unused ports, allow one known device per user port, make sure only the real DHCP server can hand out addresses, and check ARP packets against the DHCP bindings.

ip arp inspection vlan 1
interface g0/1

steps.see: Port Status Secure-shutdown and a violation count of 1, then Secure-up again after recovery.

Port security learned each PC's address as a sticky address.

With DHCP snooping on, the PCs got their addresses from the real server.

modules.title: Wireless fundamentals and secure WLANs
modules.summary: How Wi-Fi shares the airwaves, how enterprise wireless is built from access points and controllers, and how to secure a WLAN with WPA2 and WPA3.

lessons.title: Wireless principles: radio, channels and SSIDs
objectives: Describe how Wi-Fi shares radio channels, and why channel planning matters
Explain SSIDs, BSSIDs and how clients roam between access points
key_points: Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) sends data by radio in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, and 6 GHz from Wi-Fi 6E. Devices on a channel share it and take turns, using CSMA/CA to avoid collisions, so Wi-Fi is half duplex.

In the 2.4 GHz band, 20 MHz channels overlap their neighbours, so only three can sit side by side without overlapping: 1, 6 and 11 is the usual plan. The 5 GHz band has many more non-overlapping channels for neighbouring access points.

An SSID is a wireless network's name. A BSS is one access point radio and its clients, identified by the radio's MAC address (the BSSID); an ESS is several access points sharing an SSID, so clients can roam between them.

Signals weaken with distance and are absorbed, reflected and scattered by walls, water and metal, and other radios and devices such as microwave ovens interfere. Strength is measured in dBm, where closer to 0 is stronger; the signal-to-noise ratio matters as much.
802.11n is Wi-Fi 4, 802.11ac is Wi-Fi 5 (5 GHz only) and 802.11ax is Wi-Fi 6, called Wi-Fi 6E when it uses the 6 GHz band.

lessons.title: Wireless architectures: autonomous, cloud and controller-based
objectives: Compare autonomous, cloud-managed and controller-based access points
Describe CAPWAP, AP modes and how APs and controllers connect to switches
key_points: Autonomous access points are configured one at a time and each makes its own decisions, which suits small sites. Cloud-managed APs, such as Cisco Meraki, are configured and monitored from a dashboard in the cloud.

Controller-based networks pair lightweight APs with a wireless LAN controller (WLC). In this split-MAC design the AP does real-time work, such as sending beacons and acknowledging frames, and the WLC handles management, security and roaming.

Lightweight APs talk to the WLC through CAPWAP tunnels: control messages on UDP port 5246, encrypted with DTLS, and client data on UDP port 5247. An AP finds its controller by broadcast on its subnet, DHCP option 43 or DNS.

AP modes include local (the default: serve clients and tunnel their traffic to the WLC), FlexConnect (switch client traffic locally at a branch, and keep working if the WLC link fails), monitor, sniffer, rogue detector and bridge for mesh links.

A local-mode AP connects to a switch access port, since its clients' traffic travels inside CAPWAP; FlexConnect and autonomous APs connect to trunks to carry several VLANs. A WLC connects with trunks and can bundle its ports with LAG, a static EtherChannel.
Administrators manage a WLC through its console, SSH, or its web GUI over HTTPS, and a RADIUS or TACACS+ server can check their logins.

lessons.title: WPA2, WPA3 and configuring a secure WLAN
objectives: Compare WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3, and personal with enterprise authentication
Create a WPA2 WLAN with a pre-shared key in a WLC's GUI
key_points: WEP and WPA with TKIP are broken and shouldn't be used. WPA2 encrypts with AES-CCMP. WPA3 adds stronger protections and requires Protected Management Frames, which stop forged disconnect messages.

Personal mode uses one pre-shared key (PSK) for everyone. Enterprise mode authenticates each user or device with 802.1X and EAP against a RADIUS server, so one person's access can be removed without changing everyone's key.

WPA3-Personal replaces the PSK handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline guessing of the passphrase and gives forward secrecy. WPA3-Enterprise adds an optional 192-bit mode, and Enhanced Open (OWE) encrypts open networks.
With WPA2-Personal, anyone who captures a client's four-way handshake can try to guess the passphrase offline, so choose a long, random one.
On a Cisco WLC, a WLAN ties a profile name and an SSID to an interface, the VLAN its clients join. Its Security tab, under Layer 2, sets WPA2 with AES and the key management: PSK or 802.1X.

walkthrough.title: Create a WPA2-PSK WLAN on a wireless LAN controller

steps.do: From a PC on the management network, open the Web Browser, go to the WLC's management address (https://192.168.1.254, or http://192.168.1.254 if your Packet Tracer version doesn't answer on HTTPS), and log in. On a new controller you're first asked to create an admin account.
Open the WLANs menu, choose Create New from the list and click Go.
Enter Profile Name Staff and SSID Staff, keep the ID offered, and click Apply.
On the General tab, set Status to Enabled and choose the interface the clients will use: management in a small lab.

On the Security tab's Layer 2 sub-tab, choose WPA+WPA2, tick WPA2 Policy with AES encryption, enable PSK under Authentication Key Management, set PSK Format to ASCII and type a long passphrase. Click Apply.
steps.see: The WLAN saved with WPA2 and PSK.

steps.do: Open WLANs again to check it.
steps.see: Staff, enabled, with [WPA2][Auth(PSK)] as its security policy.

steps.do: On a laptop with a wireless module, open Desktop | PC Wireless, find Staff on the Connect tab, enter the passphrase and connect.
steps.see: The laptop associates with the AP and gets an address by DHCP.

steps.do: On the WLC, open MONITOR | Clients.
steps.see: The laptop's MAC address, the AP it joined and the WLAN Staff.

lab.title: Build a secure staff WLAN
lab.goal: Build a controller-based wireless network in Packet Tracer: a lightweight access point that joins a WLC, a staff WLAN secured with WPA2 and a pre-shared key, and a laptop that connects to it.
setup: The starter file r1-base.txt and the settings in wlan.txt

steps.do: Build the network in wlan.txt: R1 (2911) g0/0 to S1 (2960) g0/1, then Server0, a WLC-2504, a lightweight AP (such as the 3702i) and Admin-PC on S1's ports. Paste r1-base.txt into R1, and give Server0 and Admin-PC their static addresses.
On Server0, set up the DHCP pool from wlan.txt, including WLC Address 192.168.1.254, so the AP learns where its controller is.
Click the WLC and, on its Config tab, give its management interface the static address 192.168.1.254, mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway 192.168.1.1.
Give the laptop a wireless card: on its Physical tab, turn it off, drag out the Ethernet module, drag in a WPC300N and turn it back on.

From Admin-PC's Web Browser, open the WLC's GUI at its management address and log in, creating the admin account if this is the first visit. Under WIRELESS, check the AP appears in the list of access points.
Create the WLAN Staff: WLANs | Create New | Go, Profile Name and SSID Staff, then Apply. On the General tab set Status Enabled and the interface management.

On the Security tab, Layer 2: WPA+WPA2, WPA2 Policy with AES, PSK under Authentication Key Management, PSK Format ASCII and a passphrase of at least 16 characters. Apply, then open WLANs to check the security policy.
steps.see: Staff enabled, with [WPA2][Auth(PSK)].

steps.do: On the laptop, connect to Staff in Desktop | PC Wireless with the passphrase. Then, on its Command Prompt, check its address and reach the gateway.
steps.code:
ipconfig
ping 192.168.1.1
steps.see: A Wireless0 connection with an address from 192.168.1.100 up, and replies from 192.168.1.1.

steps.do: On the WLC, open MONITOR | Clients and find the laptop.
Write a short comparison: what would change on this WLAN, and for its users, with WPA2-Enterprise instead of a PSK, and with WPA3-Personal?

The laptop connected over wireless, got an address from the pool and reaches the gateway.
The WLC lists the laptop as a client of Staff.
The comparison explains that WPA2-Enterprise authenticates each user with 802.1X against a RADIUS server, and that WPA3-Personal replaces the PSK handshake with SAE.

project.title: Secure a branch office network
project.brief: A branch office has a staff LAN, a guest LAN, a server LAN and a wireless network for staff. Build it in Cisco Packet Tracer, reusing your labs if you like, and secure it as a whole. Harden the router and the switches: secrets and local users, SSH version 2 only and only from the admin PC, protection against password guessing, and logins checked by a TACACS+ server with a local fallback. Filter traffic with ACLs so guests can use only the web server and DNS, staff can reach everything, and management is possible only from the admin PC. Protect the access ports with port security, DHCP snooping and, where your Packet Tracer supports it, dynamic ARP inspection, and shut every unused port. Add a staff WLAN secured with WPA2 and a pre-shared key on a wireless LAN controller. Then test it the way an auditor would, recording what should work and what shouldn't, and write a one-page security assessment of the branch.
deliverables: The running configurations of the router and switches
The staff WLAN's settings from the WLC
A test table: each test (such as guest to staff PC ping, guest browsing the web server, SSH from a staff PC), what should happen, and what did, with the output that shows it

A one-page security assessment: the main threats to this branch, which vulnerabilities your controls address, what risk remains, and how you would add a site-to-site IPsec VPN to head office and move the WLAN to WPA3

rubric.name: Device hardening and AAA
rubric.description: Secrets and local users are hashed, management is SSH version 2 only from the admin PC, login protection is on, and logins use TACACS+ with a working local fallback.

rubric.name: Access control lists
rubric.description: The ACLs implement the policy exactly, are placed sensibly (standard near the destination, extended near the source), carry remarks, and the tests prove both what's allowed and what's blocked.

rubric.name: Layer 2 protections
rubric.description: User ports have port security, DHCP snooping trusts only the right ports, dynamic ARP inspection is configured or its absence explained, and unused ports are shut.

rubric.name: Secure WLAN
rubric.description: The staff WLAN uses WPA2 with AES and a long PSK, the AP joins the controller, and a wireless client connects and reaches the network.

rubric.name: Testing evidence
rubric.description: The test table covers every part of the policy, with real output for each result, including the tests that are meant to fail.

rubric.name: Security assessment
rubric.description: The assessment names realistic threats and vulnerabilities, links each to a control, is honest about remaining risk, and explains the VPN and WPA3 plans correctly.

project.submit: Paste the configurations, the WLAN settings, your test table with its output, and your security assessment. If you can share your .pkt file, add a link to it.
